title: Fixtures, soils and material compatibility
audience: Cleaners who select products and methods for bathroom and wet-area fixtures.
learningOutcomes: Identify the main fixture materials in a bathroom before selecting a product.
Distinguish soap film, mineral scale, body oils and dirt, and match each to an approved method.
Justify an exclusion where a product or method is unsuitable for the surface.

instruction.heading: Identify the material first
instruction.body: Fixtures do not respond the same way to the same product. Glazed ceramic, enamel, acrylic, chrome, stainless steel, sealed stone and unsealed natural stone each have their own sensitivity to acids, alkalis, abrasives and solvents. Before choosing a product, look at the surface, check the site record if one exists, and ask the client or supervisor if the material is uncertain. If you cannot identify it, treat it as sensitive and use the gentlest approved method.

instruction.heading: Match the soil to the method
instruction.body: Soap film, mineral scale from hard water, body oils and ordinary dirt need different approaches. Soap film is usually removed with a mild, compatible detergent. Mineral scale may need an acid-based product on suitable surfaces, but acid can etch natural stone and damage some finishes, so it must not be used on sensitive surfaces without approval. Body oils and grease respond to a degreaser that is compatible with the finish. Dirt in a joint or fixing may need a mechanical method that does not scratch the surface. One product is rarely right for every soil in the room.

instruction.heading: Reading the label and testing
instruction.body: Read the product label and SDS for intended surfaces, dilution, ventilation, PPE and contact time before use. Test on an inconspicuous area only where the manufacturer and the site procedure allow it, and wait for the test area to dry before judging the result. Never mix products, and never transfer product into an unlabelled container. Record the product name and the test result if a test is carried out.

instruction.heading: When to exclude a method
instruction.body: Some requests are outside what the cleaner should do. A client who asks for an acidic descaler on marble is asking for a method that can etch the surface. The correct response is to explain the risk, use only a stone-compatible approach that the site allows, and escalate any persistent marks to the supervisor for a specialist assessment. Excluding a method is a professional decision. Record the limitation in the job notes so the client understands what was and was not done.

procedure: Identify each fixture material before selecting a product, and treat unknown materials as sensitive.
Identify the soil type: soap film, scale, body oil or dirt.
Read the label and SDS for surface, dilution, PPE, ventilation and contact time.
Test on an inconspicuous area only where the procedure permits, and record the result.
Avoid abrasives on easily scratched finishes and acidic products on acid-sensitive natural stone.
Record any exclusion and the reason for it, and escalate persistent marks.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for an acidic scale remover on a marble vanity top with dull patches.
workedExamples.reasoning: Explain that acid can etch marble, so the acidic product is excluded. Use only the stone-compatible approach the site allows, and escalate the persistent patches for a specialist assessment. Record the limitation and the reason in the job notes.

equipmentAndPpe: Non-scratching cloths and soft brushes for finishes.
Product list with labels and SDS available on site.
Gloves and eye protection as set by the product SDS.
Ventilation check before using any product with fumes.

commonErrors.error: Using an acid product on natural stone because it removes scale quickly.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the material first and use a stone-compatible method.

commonErrors.error: Using an abrasive pad on chrome or polished stainless steel.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a non-scratching tool and check the finish first.

commonErrors.error: Mixing two products to get a stronger result.
commonErrors.prevention: Never mix products. Use one approved product at a time, rinsing as the label directs.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Product labels and SDS govern dilution, PPE, ventilation and disposal. Where a business keeps a hazardous chemicals register, each product must be listed with its current SDS under the national model WHS approach.

qualityStandard: Correct product and tool selected for at least six fixture samples and three soil types.
At least two exclusions justified with a reason.
No abrasive or acidic product used on a sensitive finish during the practical.
documentationEvidence: Product selection record for the job.
Test result and exclusion notes where a test was carried out.
summary: Identify the material before choosing a product.
Match the soil to the method, and do not use one product for everything.
Read the label and SDS, and test only where allowed.
Exclude unsuitable methods and record the reason.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which fixture is most at risk from an acidic descaler?
options: Sealed natural stone such as marble
Glazed ceramic tile on the wall
Stainless steel sink basin and tap

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the correct use of a product test on a surface?
options: Test any area that is convenient and judge the result immediately right away
Test an inconspicuous area only where the procedure allows, and wait for it to dry
Skip the test if the product label is recognised and the surface looks familiar

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must cleaning products not be mixed?
options: Mixed products cost less per clean, so the mix is kept on the trolley
Mixing only matters on natural stone
Mixing can create hazardous reactions or reduce effectiveness
